theme: Comfort in affliction; the commandments as songs
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 119:49-96. Today’s section moves from joy in the word to comfort in suffering. Notice how the psalmist speaks of affliction.
settingTheScene: The second section of the great acrostic psalm continues the theme with a new emphasis. The psalmist is under pressure from the arrogant and wicked, and he turns to God’s word for comfort. These verses include some of the most personal confessions in the psalm, as he describes his affliction and his dependence on God’s promises.
observation: “Remember your word to your servant, in which you have made me hope” (v. 49).
“This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life” (v. 50).
“Your statutes have been my songs in the house of my sojourning” (v. 54).
“I have considered my ways and turned my feet to your testimonies; I hasten and do not delay to keep your commandments” (vv. 59-60).
“It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes” (v. 71).
“I know, O LORD, that your rules are righteous, and that in faithfulness you have afflicted me” (v. 75).
“If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction” (v. 92).
“I have seen a limit to all perfection, but your commandment is exceedingly broad” (v. 96).
interpretation:
This section is a school of comfort. The psalmist is in distress, but he finds that God’s word is a comfort. “This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life.” The promise is not a vague hope. It is a specific word that God has spoken, and it has the power to give life when everything else seems to be dying.

Verses 54 and 55 are striking. The psalmist calls God’s statutes “songs” in the house of his sojourning. A traveler’s house might be a poor place, but it is filled with song. The word can turn any dwelling into a place of worship. And at night, he remembers God’s name and keeps his law.

The center of the section is verses 67, 71, and 75, where the psalmist reflects on his suffering. “Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word.” “It is good for me that I was afflicted.” It is a hard thing to say, and he does not say it lightly. But he has learned that his troubles were God’s way of teaching him. In faithfulness, God has afflicted him. Affliction was not a sign of God’s absence. It was a form of his care.

This is not a general claim that all suffering is God’s discipline. The psalmist is speaking from his own experience, and he is not claiming to be sinless. But he points to a truth that the whole Bible affirms: God uses hardship to draw us closer to himself. As Hebrews 12:10-11 says, he disciplines us “for our good, that we may share his holiness.”

The section ends with a sweeping statement of the word’s scope: “I have seen a limit to all perfection, but your commandment is exceedingly broad.” Everything else in life has limits. The word of God does not. There is always more to learn, and more to love.
connection: Paul says that “suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope” (Romans 5:3-4). Hebrews 12:5-11 quotes Proverbs about the Lord’s discipline. Jesus is the one who “learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). Jesus said, “These things I have spoken to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).
application:
Think of a hard time that taught you something about God. Thank him for it.

Choose one promise from Scripture to hold on to in a current difficulty.

Sing or hum a psalm as you go about your day, as the psalmist did in the house of his sojourning.
prayerPrompts: Tell God where you need his promise to give you life.
Thank him for what he has taught you in affliction.
Ask him to make his commands your songs.
